# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

4. Counter store: Redis vs local memory. Facts: 3 instances, LB round-robin → local memory gives 3× effective limit. Recommend Redis.

6. Fail-open vs fail-closed when Redis unreachable.
7. Rejected response shape: 429 + Retry-After + body? Headers?
8. Limits/numbers: what rate limits for normal/enterprise; who owns the numbers.
9. Enterprise higher limits mechanism: config file, DB, Redis config, per-customer table.
10. Rollout: shadow mode (count-only log), gradual %, hard cut, whitelist during rollout.
11. Also burst: token bucket burst size vs sustained rate — part of algorithm numbers.
12. Timeout for Redis calls (latency budget on hot path).

brief.what: Endpoints in scope: POST /orders only, GET /orders too, or everything on the server
brief.where: PLAN.md line 9: POST is the expensive call, GET is cheap. src/server.ts has exactly two routes.

options.description: POST is the expensive call; GET stays unthrottled
options.label: POST /orders only
options.tradeoff: Protects the Postgres hot spot, zero risk to cheap reads, but runaway queries can still hammer the DB

options.description: POST limits tight, GET limits loose (e.g. 10x higher)
options.label: Both endpoints
options.tradeoff: Full protection, but doubles the limits to define and explain to integrators

options.description: One global bucket per customer
options.label: Everything uniformly
options.tradeoff: Simplest to reason about, but a GET script can starve POST quota

brief.how: Decides the counter key and whether the 401 flood path is rate-limited at all. If you want the IP fallback you also inherit NAT collisions (many customers behind one office IP).
brief.what: Key: x-customer-id, client IP, or both
brief.where: PLAN.md lists this as undecided. Fact from src/server.ts:7-8: x-customer-id is a plain client-asserted header with no token check, and requests without it already get 401. So the 40k-order script authenticated itself; IP is only a fallback for header-less junk.

options.description: Current behavior already uses it; IP/spec appeals get manually reviewed
options.label: Yes, customer ID, plus spec-fallback review
options.tradeoff: Simple and matches who you can actually bill/talk to; occasional false positives on malformed headers

options.description: Counters keyed x-customer-id + client IP
options.label: Customer ID, downgraded to IP when header is missing/invalid
options.tradeoff: Handles the 401 flood path, but shared NAT IPs can collide into one bucket

options.description: Two independent limits, both must pass
options.label: Both always (AND)
options.tradeoff: Strictest, but multiplies tooling: customers behind office NATs hit the IP limit as a shared pool

brief.how: In-memory under round-robin means each customer effectively gets 3x the configured limit and per-instance drift; Redis is the only shared truth on 3 instances. Reusing the session cluster couples the rate limiter's fail mode to another service's cache.
brief.what: Do we reuse the Redis 7 cluster that sessions already use, run a separate one, or keep counters in instance memory
brief.where: PLAN.md: 3 instances behind round-robin LB, Redis cluster already exists for sessions by another service.

options.description: Same cluster, keys prefixed rl: and timeouts enforced
options.label: Yes, existing Redis, namespaced keys
options.tradeoff: No new infra this week, but a rate-limit latency spike or hot key shares fate with the other service

options.description: Dedicated instance/namespace for rate limiting
options.label: Yes, but a separate Redis
options.tradeoff: Blast-radius isolation, but provisioning a new Redis this week is the long pole

options.description: Each of 3 instances counts independently; effective limit becomes 3x what you set under round-robin LB
options.label: No - in-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: Zero network latency and no Redis dependency, but the limit isn't actually a limit: under round-robin a script gets N x 3 requests

brief.how: Sets the failure coupling between Redis health and order availability. Shapes ops: either way you need an alert on degraded mode.
brief.what: When the counter store is unreachable, allow the request or reject it
brief.where: PLAN.md lists this undecided. If you picked in-memory in the previous step this is almost moot (answer anyway; it also covers Postgres being slow mid-request).

options.description: On Redis timeout/error, count locally as approximation or just allow
options.label: Fail-open
options.tradeoff: Availability preserved; a Redis outage re-opens the 40k-order flood exactly when you're firefighting it

options.description: Reject with 503 when the counter is unreachable
options.label: Fail-closed
options.tradeoff: Protection intact, but Redis blips now 5xx every order endpoint - worse blast radius than the problem being solved

options.description: Fail open, but log >N req/min per customer during degraded mode
options.label: Fail-open + alert loudly on degradation
options.tradeoff: Keeps orders flowing and still detects abuse during outages, but needs a log/alert sink

brief.how: Bursty-but-legit traffic is exactly where fixed window's boundary effect (up to ~2x limit at window edges) and token bucket's burst credit differ. Choice also determines what Retry-After you can compute.
brief.what: Fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket
brief.where: PLAN.md undecided. Fact: ~20 enterprise customers legitimately burst, which is the whole reason this is delicate.

options.description: Redis INCR + EXPIRE, ~2 commands, well-understood
options.label: Yes - fixed window
options.tradeoff: Cheapest and easiest to reason about/retry against; boundary burst can admit roughly 2x limit at window edges

options.description: Accurate average, no edge burst
options.label: Sliding window (approximate, two timestamps)
options.tradeoff: Smooths the boundary problem, ~2x the Redis work and harder to explain Retry-After

options.description: Limits sustained rate AND burst; keeps the 'legit burst' behavior
options.label: No - token bucket
options.tradeoff: Best fit for scripted bursts, but needs Lua/atomic refill, more tuning knobs, and Retry-After is approximate

brief.how: Ownership decides whether raising a limit is a deploy, a config change, or an email to another team. Numbers decide who breaks on launch day.
brief.what: Who owns the limit numbers - engineering defaults, or per-customer contracts
brief.where: PLAN.md: 'who owns those numbers' is explicitly undecided; ~20 enterprise customers with scripted bursts.

options.description: You or the team on-call owns the current numbers; revisit after a month of data
options.label: Yes - you set them from today's data, team owns them
options.tradeoff: Fast, but none of the 20 enterprises were consulted before their scripts suddenly 429

options.description: Buckets become a contract; account management owns exceptions entirely
options.label: Yes - but published as a documented contract
options.tradeoff: Predictable for integrators and frees you from ad-hoc approvals; changes become a process, not a deploy

options.description: Enterprise numbers set per-customer through account management
options.label: No - engineering owns infrastructure defaults, accounts owns per-customer overrides
options.tradeoff: Right incentive split, but you need an escalation path defined before launch

brief.how: Decides who can change a limit at what speed and whether support/engineering need each other.
brief.what: Mechanism for higher enterprise limits: hardcoded tiers, config file, DB rows, or Redis keys
brief.where: PLAN.md: 'How enterprise customers get higher limits' undecided; default tier(s) will be decided in the next round once this mechanism exists.

options.description: File or Postgres table per customer; re-read on change
options.label: Yes - per-customer config (DB table or config file)
options.tradeoff: No code deploys to raise a limit; adds one lookup per request (cacheable)

options.description: Serve limits from Redis keys; support sets them
options.label: Serve limits from Redis keys
options.tradeoff: Instant take-effect with zero deploys, but now the config channel is the same store you fail over on

options.description: Shipped as code constants; PR to change
options.label: No - two hardcoded tiers, PR to change
options.tradeoff: Zero extra machinery this week, but every enterprise exception is a deploy and a review

brief.how: 429 + Retry-After is the standard scripts and HTTP libraries already honor; 503 gets conflated with server outage by retry logic.
brief.what: What a rejected client sees: status code, headers, body shape
brief.where: PLAN.md undecided. src/server.ts currently returns plain-text responses for 401/404, so there is no existing error-body convention to preserve.

options.description: Industry-standard; scripted integrators already handle it
options.label: 429 + Retry-After header + machine-readable body
options.tradeoff: A few lines of extra code; old naive scripts may just retry immediately in a tight loop - they need exponential backoff guidance in docs

options.description: Body only; simplest
options.label: 429 with body, no headers
options.tradeoff: Minimal, but scripts can't back off intelligently and will poll

options.description: Match reads like a bug report
options.label: 503 instead of 429
options.tradeoff: Some frameworks auto-retry 503; misleading semantics

brief.how: Shadow mode turns wrong limit guesses into log lines instead of broken customer scripts; the cost is a week of delay.
brief.what: Rollout strategy: shadow (log-only) first, gradual enforcement, or hard enable with exceptions
brief.where: PLAN.md lists rollout as undecided, and the plan ships this week. 20 enterprise integrators were not consulted (they learn about it when they hit a 429).

options.description: Ship counting first, review the log for violators, then flip enforcement
options.label: Yes - shadow mode (log-only) for a week, then enforce
options.tradeoff: No integrator breaks; delays enforcement by a week (you said ship this week - counting ships, blocking waits)

options.description: Mispredicted burst profiles cause 429s in production scripts with minutes of warning
options.label: No - enforce immediately with per-customer exceptions for top talkers
options.tradeoff: Fastest to real protection; any limit you guessed wrong breaks that customer's script today

options.description: Sample of traffic pays the cost of your tuning
options.label: No - enforce on ~5% of requests for the first days
options.tradeoff: Limits breakage risk, but sampling itself breaks per-customer burst expectations and is confusing to debug

arguments.i: Grilling PLAN.md - round 1 of rate-limiting design

brief.how: Decides how many limit buckets and rate configs you maintain. Cheap calls can still amplify under loops, so protection breadth is a real choice.
brief.what: Endpoints in scope: POST /orders only, GET /orders too, or everything on the server
brief.where: PLAN.md line 9: POST is the expensive call, GET is cheap. src/server.ts has exactly two routes.

options.description: POST is the expensive call; GET stays unthrottled
options.label: POST /orders only
options.tradeoff: Protects the Postgres hot spot, zero risk to cheap reads, but runaway queries can still hammer the DB

options.description: POST limits tight, GET limits loose (e.g. 10x higher)
options.label: Both endpoints
options.tradeoff: Full protection, but doubles the limits to define and explain to integrators

options.description: One global bucket per customer
options.label: Everything uniformly
options.tradeoff: Simplest to reason about, but a GET script can starve POST quota

questions.question: Should the limit apply to both POST and GET /orders, with GET allowed a much higher rate than POST?

brief.how: Decides the counter key and whether the 401 flood path is rate-limited at all. If you want the IP fallback you also inherit NAT collisions (many customers behind one office IP).
brief.what: Key: x-customer-id, client IP, or both
brief.where: PLAN.md lists this as undecided. Fact from src/server.ts:7-8: x-customer-id is a plain client-asserted header with no token check, and requests without it already get 401. So the 40k-order script authenticated itself; IP is only a fallback for header-less junk.

options.description: Current behavior already uses it; IP/spec appeals get manually reviewed
options.label: Yes, customer ID only
options.tradeoff: Simple and matches who you can actually bill/talk to; the header-less flood path stays unthrottled

options.description: Counters keyed x-customer-id + client IP
options.label: Customer ID, downgraded to IP when header is missing/invalid
options.tradeoff: Handles the 401 flood path too, but shared NAT IPs can collide into one bucket

options.description: Two independent limits, both must pass
options.label: Both always (AND)
options.tradeoff: Strictest, but multiplies tooling: customers behind office NATs hit the IP limit as a shared pool

questions.question: Should the limit key on x-customer-id only (the header the server already requires)?

brief.how: In-memory under round-robin means each customer effectively gets 3x the configured limit and per-instance drift; Redis is the only shared truth on 3 instances. Reusing the session cluster couples the rate limiter's fail mode to another service's cache.
brief.what: Do we reuse the Redis 7 cluster that sessions already use, run a separate one, or keep counters in instance memory
brief.where: PLAN.md: 3 instances behind round-robin LB, Redis cluster already exists for sessions by another service.

options.description: Same cluster, keys prefixed rl: and timeouts enforced
options.label: Yes, existing Redis, namespaced keys
options.tradeoff: No new infra this week, but a rate-limit latency spike or hot key shares fate with the other service

options.description: Dedicated instance/namespace for rate limiting
options.label: Yes, but a separate Redis
options.tradeoff: Blast-radius isolation, but provisioning a new Redis this week is the long pole

options.description: Each of 3 instances counts independently; effective limit becomes 3x what you set under round-robin LB
options.label: No - in-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: Zero network latency and no Redis dependency, but the limit isn't actually a limit: under round-robin a script gets N x 3 requests

questions.question: Do counters live in the existing Redis cluster (namespaced keys, no new infrastructure)?

brief.how: Sets the failure coupling between Redis health and order availability. Shapes ops: either way you need an alert on degraded mode.
brief.what: When the counter store is unreachable, allow the request or reject it
brief.where: PLAN.md lists this undecided. If you picked in-memory in the previous step this is almost moot (answer anyway; it also covers Postgres being slow mid-request).

options.description: On Redis timeout/error, count locally as approximation or just allow
options.label: Fail-open
options.tradeoff: Availability preserved; a Redis outage re-opens the 40k-order flood exactly when you're firefighting it

options.description: Reject with 503 when the counter is unreachable
options.label: Fail-closed
options.tradeoff: Protection intact, but Redis blips now 5xx every order endpoint - worse blast radius than the problem being solved

options.description: Fail open, but log >N req/min per customer during degraded mode
options.label: Fail-open + alert loudly on degradation
options.tradeoff: Keeps orders flowing and still detects abuse during outages, but needs a log/alert sink

questions.question: If Redis is unreachable, should requests pass through unfettered while an alert fires?

brief.how: Bursty-but-legit traffic is exactly where fixed window's boundary effect (up to ~2x limit at window edges) and token bucket's burst credit differ. Choice also determines what Retry-After you can compute.
brief.what: Fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket
brief.where: PLAN.md undecided. Fact: ~20 enterprise customers legitimately burst, which is the whole reason this is delicate.

options.description: Redis INCR + EXPIRE, ~2 commands, well-understood
options.label: Yes - fixed window
options.tradeoff: Cheapest and easiest to reason about/retry against; boundary burst can admit roughly 2x limit at window edges

options.description: Accurate average, no edge burst
options.label: Sliding window (approximate, two timestamps)
options.tradeoff: Smooths the boundary problem, ~2x the Redis work and harder to explain Retry-After

options.description: Limits sustained rate AND burst; keeps the 'legit burst' behavior
options.label: No - token bucket
options.tradeoff: Best fit for scripted bursts, but needs Lua/atomic refill, more tuning knobs, and Retry-After is approximate

questions.question: Do you reject fixed window and use a token bucket, to honor bursty-but-legit enterprise traffic while capping sustained rate?

brief.how: Ownership decides whether raising a limit is a deploy, a config change, or an email to another team. Numbers decide who breaks on launch day.
brief.what: Who owns the limit numbers - engineering defaults, or per-customer contracts
brief.where: PLAN.md: 'who owns those numbers' is explicitly undecided; ~20 enterprise customers with scripted bursts.

options.description: You or the team on-call owns the current numbers; revisit after a month of data
options.label: Yes - you set them from today's data, team owns them
options.tradeoff: Fast, but none of the 20 enterprises were consulted before their scripts suddenly 429

options.description: Buckets become a contract; account management owns exceptions entirely
options.label: Yes - but published as a documented contract
options.tradeoff: Predictable for integrators and frees you from ad-hoc approvals; changes become a process, not a deploy

options.description: Enterprise numbers set per-customer through account management
options.label: No - engineering owns infrastructure defaults, accounts owns per-customer overrides
options.tradeoff: Right incentive split, but you need an escalation path defined before launch

questions.question: Should engineering own the default limits while account management owns per-customer enterprise overrides?

brief.how: Decides who can change a limit at what speed and whether support/engineering need each other.
brief.what: Mechanism for higher enterprise limits: hardcoded tiers, config file, DB rows, or Redis keys
brief.where: PLAN.md: 'How enterprise customers get higher limits' undecided; default tier(s) will be decided in the next round once this mechanism exists.

options.description: Per-customer limits from a Postgres table or config file, cached in-process
options.label: Runtime config (DB row or config file)
options.tradeoff: No code deploys to raise a limit; adds one lookup per request (cacheable)

options.description: Serve limits from Redis keys; support sets them
options.label: Limits in Redis keys
options.tradeoff: Instant take-effect with zero deploys, but now the config channel is the same store you fail over on

options.description: Shipped as code constants; PR to change
options.label: Hardcoded tiers, PR to change
options.tradeoff: Zero extra machinery this week, but every enterprise exception is a deploy and a review

questions.question: Should per-customer limits be runtime configuration (Postgres row or config file), so raising one is not a code deploy?

brief.how: 429 + Retry-After is the standard scripts and HTTP libraries already honor; 503 gets conflated with server outage by retry logic.
brief.what: What a rejected client sees: status code, headers, body shape
brief.where: PLAN.md undecided. src/server.ts currently returns plain-text responses for 401/404, so there is no existing error-body convention to preserve.

options.description: Industry-standard; scripted integrators already handle it
options.label: 429 + Retry-After header + machine-readable body
options.tradeoff: A few lines of extra code; old naive scripts may just retry immediately in a tight loop - they need exponential backoff guidance in docs

options.description: Body only; simplest
options.label: 429 with body, no headers
options.tradeoff: Minimal, but scripts can't back off intelligently and will poll

options.description: Match reads like a bug report
options.label: 503 instead of 429
options.tradeoff: Some frameworks auto-retry 503; misleading semantics

questions.question: Should a rejected request return 429 with a Retry-After header and a machine-readable body?

brief.how: Shadow mode turns wrong limit guesses into log lines instead of broken customer scripts; the cost is a week of delay.
brief.what: Rollout strategy: shadow (log-only) first, gradual enforcement, or hard enable with exceptions
brief.where: PLAN.md lists rollout as undecided, and the plan ships this week. 20 enterprise integrators were not consulted (they learn about it when they hit a 429).

options.description: Ship counting first, review the log for violators, then flip enforcement
options.label: Yes - shadow mode (log-only) for a week, then enforce
options.tradeoff: No integrator breaks; delays enforcement by a week (you said ship this week - counting ships, blocking waits)

options.description: Mispredicted burst profiles cause 429s in production scripts with minutes of warning
options.label: No - enforce immediately with per-customer exceptions for top talkers
options.tradeoff: Fastest to real protection; any limit you guessed wrong breaks that customer's script today

options.description: Sample of traffic pays the cost of your tuning
options.label: No - enforce on ~5% of requests for the first days
options.tradeoff: Limits breakage risk, but sampling itself breaks per-customer burst expectations and is confusing to debug

questions.question: Should we ship in shadow mode first (count and log only), then flip enforcement after the log confirms who exceeds the limits?

brief.how: Decides how many limit buckets and rate configs you maintain. Cheap calls can still amplify under loops, so protection breadth is a real choice.
brief.what: Endpoints in scope: POST /orders only, GET /orders too, or everything on the server
brief.where: PLAN.md line 9: POST is the expensive call, GET is cheap. src/server.ts has exactly two routes.

options.description: POST is the expensive call; GET stays unthrottled
options.label: POST /orders only
options.tradeoff: Protects the Postgres hot spot, zero risk to cheap reads, but runaway queries can still hammer the DB

options.description: POST limits tight, GET limits loose (e.g. 10x higher)
options.label: Both endpoints
options.tradeoff: Full protection, but doubles the limits to define and explain to integrators

options.description: One global bucket per customer
options.label: Everything uniformly
options.tradeoff: Simplest to reason about, but a GET script can starve POST quota

questions.question: Should the limit apply to both POST and GET /orders, with GET allowed a much higher rate than POST?

brief.how: Decides the counter key and whether the 401 flood path is rate-limited at all. If you want the IP fallback you also inherit NAT collisions (many customers behind one office IP).
brief.what: Key: x-customer-id, client IP, or both
brief.where: PLAN.md lists this as undecided. Fact from src/server.ts:7-8: x-customer-id is a plain client-asserted header with no token check, and requests without it already get 401. So the 40k-order script authenticated itself; IP is only a fallback for header-less junk.

options.description: Current behavior already uses it; IP/spec appeals get manually reviewed
options.label: Yes, customer ID only
options.tradeoff: Simple and matches who you can actually bill/talk to; the header-less flood path stays unthrottled

options.description: Counters keyed x-customer-id + client IP
options.label: Customer ID, downgraded to IP when header is missing/invalid
options.tradeoff: Handles the 401 flood path too, but shared NAT IPs can collide into one bucket

options.description: Two independent limits, both must pass
options.label: Both always (AND)
options.tradeoff: Strictest, but multiplies tooling: customers behind office NATs hit the IP limit as a shared pool

questions.question: Should the limit key on x-customer-id only (the header the server already requires)?

brief.how: In-memory under round-robin means each customer effectively gets 3x the configured limit and per-instance drift; Redis is the only shared truth on 3 instances. Reusing the session cluster couples the rate limiter's fail mode to another service's cache.
brief.what: Do we reuse the Redis 7 cluster that sessions already use, run a separate one, or keep counters in instance memory
brief.where: PLAN.md: 3 instances behind round-robin LB, Redis cluster already exists for sessions by another service.

options.description: Same cluster, keys prefixed rl: and timeouts enforced
options.label: Yes, existing Redis, namespaced keys
options.tradeoff: No new infra this week, but a rate-limit latency spike or hot key shares fate with the other service

options.description: Dedicated instance/namespace for rate limiting
options.label: Yes, but a separate Redis
options.tradeoff: Blast-radius isolation, but provisioning a new Redis this week is the long pole

options.description: Each of 3 instances counts independently; effective limit becomes 3x what you set under round-robin LB
options.label: No - in-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: Zero network latency and no Redis dependency, but the limit isn't actually a limit: under round-robin a script gets N x 3 requests

questions.question: Do counters live in the existing Redis cluster (namespaced keys, no new infrastructure)?

brief.how: Sets the failure coupling between Redis health and order availability. Shapes ops: either way you need an alert on degraded mode.
brief.what: When the counter store is unreachable, allow the request or reject it
brief.where: PLAN.md lists this undecided. If you picked in-memory in the previous step this is almost moot (answer anyway; it also covers Postgres being slow mid-request).

options.description: On Redis timeout/error, count locally as approximation or just allow
options.label: Fail-open
options.tradeoff: Availability preserved; a Redis outage re-opens the 40k-order flood exactly when you're firefighting it

options.description: Reject with 503 when the counter is unreachable
options.label: Fail-closed
options.tradeoff: Protection intact, but Redis blips now 5xx every order endpoint - worse blast radius than the problem being solved

options.description: Fail open, but log >N req/min per customer during degraded mode
options.label: Fail-open + alert loudly on degradation
options.tradeoff: Keeps orders flowing and still detects abuse during outages, but needs a log/alert sink

questions.question: If Redis is unreachable, should requests pass through unfettered while an alert fires?

brief.how: Bursty-but-legit traffic is exactly where fixed window's boundary effect (up to ~2x limit at window edges) and token bucket's burst credit differ. Choice also determines what Retry-After you can compute.
brief.what: Fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket
brief.where: PLAN.md undecided. Fact: ~20 enterprise customers legitimately burst, which is the whole reason this is delicate.

options.description: Redis INCR + EXPIRE, ~2 commands, well-understood
options.label: Yes - fixed window
options.tradeoff: Cheapest and easiest to reason about/retry against; boundary burst can admit roughly 2x limit at window edges

options.description: Accurate average, no edge burst
options.label: Sliding window (approximate, two timestamps)
options.tradeoff: Smooths the boundary problem, ~2x the Redis work and harder to explain Retry-After

options.description: Limits sustained rate AND burst; keeps the 'legit burst' behavior
options.label: No - token bucket
options.tradeoff: Best fit for scripted bursts, but needs Lua/atomic refill, more tuning knobs, and Retry-After is approximate

questions.question: Do you reject fixed window and use a token bucket, to honor bursty-but-legit enterprise traffic while capping sustained rate?

brief.how: Ownership decides whether raising a limit is a deploy, a config change, or an email to another team. Numbers decide who breaks on launch day.
brief.what: Who owns the limit numbers - engineering defaults, or per-customer contracts
brief.where: PLAN.md: 'who owns those numbers' is explicitly undecided; ~20 enterprise customers with scripted bursts.

options.description: You or the team on-call owns the current numbers; revisit after a month of data
options.label: Yes - you set them from today's data, team owns them
options.tradeoff: Fast, but none of the 20 enterprises were consulted before their scripts suddenly 429

options.description: Buckets become a contract; account management owns exceptions entirely
options.label: Yes - but published as a documented contract
options.tradeoff: Predictable for integrators and frees you from ad-hoc approvals; changes become a process, not a deploy

options.description: Enterprise numbers set per-customer through account management
options.label: No - engineering owns infrastructure defaults, accounts owns per-customer overrides
options.tradeoff: Right incentive split, but you need an escalation path defined before launch

questions.question: Should engineering own the default limits while account management owns per-customer enterprise overrides?

brief.how: Decides who can change a limit at what speed and whether support/engineering need each other.
brief.what: Mechanism for higher enterprise limits: hardcoded tiers, config file, DB rows, or Redis keys
brief.where: PLAN.md: 'How enterprise customers get higher limits' undecided; default tier(s) will be decided in the next round once this mechanism exists.

options.description: Per-customer limits from a Postgres table or config file, cached in-process
options.label: Runtime config (DB row or config file)
options.tradeoff: No code deploys to raise a limit; adds one lookup per request (cacheable)

options.description: Serve limits from Redis keys; support sets them
options.label: Limits in Redis keys
options.tradeoff: Instant take-effect with zero deploys, but now the config channel is the same store you fail over on

options.description: Shipped as code constants; PR to change
options.label: Hardcoded tiers, PR to change
options.tradeoff: Zero extra machinery this week, but every enterprise exception is a deploy and a review

questions.question: Should per-customer limits be runtime configuration (Postgres row or config file), so raising one is not a code deploy?

brief.how: 429 + Retry-After is the standard scripts and HTTP libraries already honor; 503 gets conflated with server outage by retry logic.
brief.what: What a rejected client sees: status code, headers, body shape
brief.where: PLAN.md undecided. src/server.ts currently returns plain-text responses for 401/404, so there is no existing error-body convention to preserve.

options.description: Industry-standard; scripted integrators already handle it
options.label: 429 + Retry-After header + machine-readable body
options.tradeoff: A few lines of extra code; old naive scripts may just retry immediately in a tight loop - they need exponential backoff guidance in docs

options.description: Body only; simplest
options.label: 429 with body, no headers
options.tradeoff: Minimal, but scripts can't back off intelligently and will poll

options.description: Match reads like a bug report
options.label: 503 instead of 429
options.tradeoff: Some frameworks auto-retry 503; misleading semantics

questions.question: Should a rejected request return 429 with a Retry-After header and a machine-readable body?

brief.how: Shadow mode turns wrong limit guesses into log lines instead of broken customer scripts; the cost is a week of delay.
brief.what: Rollout strategy: shadow (log-only) first, gradual enforcement, or hard enable with exceptions
brief.where: PLAN.md lists rollout as undecided, and the plan ships this week. 20 enterprise integrators were not consulted (they learn about it when they hit a 429).

options.description: Ship counting first, review the log for violators, then flip enforcement
options.label: Yes - shadow mode (log-only) for a week, then enforce
options.tradeoff: No integrator breaks; delays enforcement by a week (you said ship this week - counting ships, blocking waits)

options.description: Mispredicted burst profiles cause 429s in production scripts with minutes of warning
options.label: No - enforce immediately with per-customer exceptions for top talkers
options.tradeoff: Fastest to real protection; any limit you guessed wrong breaks that customer's script today

options.description: Sample of traffic pays the cost of your tuning
options.label: No - enforce on ~5% of requests for the first days
options.tradeoff: Limits breakage risk, but sampling itself breaks per-customer burst expectations and is confusing to debug

questions.question: Should we ship in shadow mode first (count and log only), then flip enforcement after the log confirms who exceeds the limits?
